concept.name: Positive convexity
concept.definition: A property of a bond whose price-yield relationship is convex: prices rise more when yields fall and fall less when yields rise than duration alone predicts. All standard non-callable fixed-rate bonds exhibit positive convexity; the effect grows with longer maturity and lower coupons.
concept.intuition: The bond's price accelerates in your favor: you gain a bit extra when rates fall and lose a bit less when rates rise, compared with the straight-line duration estimate.
concept.mechanics: Convexity is the curvature (second derivative) of the price-yield function; with positive convexity, duration falls as yields rise and rises as yields fall. The effect is most pronounced in long-duration, low-coupon bonds, and the price impact is captured by adding a convexity adjustment to the duration estimate.
concept.formula: Convexity ≈ (P(−) + P(+) − 2 × P_0) / (P_0 × Δy²) > 0; price change ≈ −ModDur × Δy × P_0 + ½ × Convexity × (Δy)² × P_0.
concept.failure_modes: Convexity benefits are already priced in (higher-convexity bonds trade at lower yields), so it is not a free advantage; for small rate moves the convexity term is negligible and adds little to the duration estimate.
concept.misconceptions: Positive convexity is not a guarantee of outperformance and does not mean prices cannot fall; it only describes the curvature of the price-yield relationship.
concept.example: A 30-year zero-coupon bond has very high positive convexity: a 100 bp yield decline lifts its price by more than duration suggests, while a 100 bp rise costs it less.

citations.source: Fidelity, Duration: Understanding the Relationship Between Bond Prices and Interest Rates
citations.section: Using a bond's convexity to gauge interest rate risk
